nameStory: The White Cylichna gets its name from its pristine, porcelain-white shell that stands out against the muddy seafloor where it lives. The genus name 'Cylichna' comes from the Greek word for 'cylinder,' referring to the shell's distinctive elongated, tube-like shape that looks almost like a tiny white pill.
description: The White Cylichna is a small sea snail that belongs to a group called bubble snails, though it lacks the typical bubble-like appearance of its relatives. Instead, it has a smooth, cylindrical white shell that's about the size of a rice grain, typically reaching only 3-6 millimeters long. This tiny marine mollusk lives buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms, where it hunts for even smaller prey using a hidden, extendable proboscis. Unlike typical snails, you'll rarely see the animal itself—just the distinctive white shell washing up on beaches.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Perfectly cylindrical and smooth, like a tiny white medicine capsule with rounded ends—no spiral pattern visible from the outside

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pure white or cream-colored shell with a glossy, almost porcelain-like finish that feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically 3-6mm long—about the size of a single grain of rice or small pill

idTips.label: Opening
idTips.description: Narrow slit-like opening that runs almost the full length of one side, unlike the round opening of typical snails

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Shell feels solid and smooth with no ridges, bumps, or growth lines—like touching a polished bead

habitat: White Cylichna lives in sandy and muddy bottoms in deeper coastal waters of the North Atlantic. In New England waters, it's typically found offshore in depths of 20-200 feet, though empty shells occasionally wash up on sandy beaches after storms. Look for shells mixed in with other small marine debris along the high tide line on beaches from Maine to Cape Cod.

seasonality.spring: Best time to find shells on beaches as spring storms stir up the seafloor and wash specimens ashore. Living animals are active in deeper waters but rarely seen by casual observers.
seasonality.summer: Shells may be found on beaches year-round, but are less common as calmer seas mean less stirring of deep-water sediments. Peak breeding season occurs in deeper waters.
seasonality.fall: Another good season for finding shells on beaches as autumn storms become more frequent. Storm-tossed shells are often the freshest and most intact specimens.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms can bring shells ashore, but harsh conditions make beach combing challenging. Animals remain active in deeper waters where temperatures are more stable.

funFact: Despite being a snail, the White Cylichna is actually a fierce predator that can turn its throat inside-out like a sock to grab prey larger than its shell opening—imagine if you could turn your entire throat into an extendable grabbing arm!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with small bits of white plastic or pill fragments on the beach, but the White Cylichna shell has a natural glossy sheen and the distinctive long, narrow opening that runs down one side. Memory trick: "Cylichna's cylinder has a crack down the side."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "bubble snail," the White Cylichna doesn't actually have a bubble-shaped shell like many of its relatives. This is a common source of confusion for shell collectors who expect all bubble snails to look bubbly—the White Cylichna proves that common family names don't always describe every member perfectly.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM - Limited data available]** Since this appears to be the only Cylichna species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other small white shells like tiny moon snails or dove shells. Unlike moon snails which show clear spiral patterns, the White Cylichna appears perfectly cylindrical with no visible spiraling from the outside. Dove shells are more cone-shaped rather than cylindrical and have round rather than slit-like openings.
